1.uses: Ammonia production (Haber–Bosch process), oil refining, hydrogenation of oils and rocket fuel.
1.fact: It is the most abundant element in the universe: about three quarters of the mass of ordinary matter.

2.uses: Balloons and airships, cooling superconducting magnets (MRI scanners), diving gas mixtures and welding.
2.fact: It was detected in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, before being found on Earth; its name comes from the Greek helios, 'sun'.

3.uses: Lithium-ion batteries, special glasses and ceramics, lubricating greases and mood-stabilizing medicines.
3.fact: It is the least dense metal: it floats on water.

4.uses: X-ray–transparent windows, non-sparking copper–beryllium alloys and space telescope mirrors.
4.fact: The James Webb Space Telescope's mirrors are made of beryllium coated with a thin layer of gold.

5.uses: Heat-resistant borosilicate glass, nuclear reactor control rods (boron-10), lightweight fibers and detergents (borax).
5.fact: Its compounds give fireworks and flares a green flame.

6.uses: Steel (an iron–carbon alloy), graphite in pencils and batteries, industrial diamonds, carbon fiber and fuels.
6.fact: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon: only the arrangement of their atoms differs.

7.uses: Ammonia for fertilizers and explosives, inert atmospheres in the food and electronics industries, and liquid nitrogen as a coolant.
7.fact: It makes up about 78% of the air we breathe, by volume.

8.uses: Steelmaking, oxy-acetylene welding, medical oxygen and, together with liquid hydrogen, rocket propulsion.
8.fact: It is the most abundant element in Earth's crust: almost half of its mass.

9.uses: Toothpaste and fluoridated water against tooth decay, Teflon, refrigerants and uranium enrichment (UF₆).
9.fact: It is the most electronegative element and one of the most reactive: it even attacks glass.

10.uses: Illuminated signs, helium–neon lasers, high-voltage indicators and cryogenic cooling.
10.fact: It is so inert that no stable neon compound is known.

11.uses: Table salt, baking soda and caustic soda; sodium-vapor street lamps and nuclear reactor coolant.
11.fact: It is a metal soft enough to cut with a knife, and it reacts violently with water.

12.uses: Lightweight alloys with aluminum for cars and aircraft, flares and fireworks, antacids and supplements.
12.fact: Every chlorophyll molecule has a magnesium atom at its center.

13.uses: Cans, foil, aircraft, construction, high-voltage power lines and cookware.
13.fact: It was a precious metal, pricier than silver, until the Hall–Héroult process made it cheap to produce in 1886.

14.uses: Computer chips and solar panels (high-purity silicon), glass, cement, ceramics and silicones.
14.fact: Silicon Valley, California's tech hub, is named after this element.

15.uses: Fertilizers, safety matches, detergents and food additives; it is part of DNA and bones.
15.fact: Hennig Brand obtained it from urine in 1669: it is the first element with a known discoverer.

16.uses: Sulfuric acid production, rubber vulcanization, fertilizers, fungicides and gunpowder.
16.fact: The 'rotten egg' smell is not pure sulfur but hydrogen sulfide (H₂S).

17.uses: Drinking water and pool disinfection, PVC, bleach and the synthesis of medicines.
17.fact: With sodium it forms table salt, even though both elements are dangerous on their own.

18.uses: Inert atmosphere for welding, incandescent and fluorescent lamps, and semiconductor manufacturing.
18.fact: It is the third most abundant gas in air; its name means 'lazy' in Greek.

19.uses: Fertilizers (potassium chloride), soaps, glass and salt substitutes.
19.fact: It is essential for nerve and muscle function.

20.uses: Cement, lime and plaster; metal refining and dietary supplements.
20.fact: It is the most abundant metal in the human body: it is part of bones and teeth.

21.uses: Aluminum–scandium alloys for bicycle frames and sports equipment, and metal-halide lamps.
21.fact: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-boron' before it was discovered in 1879.

22.uses: Aircraft, medical implants and prostheses, and titanium dioxide as a white pigment in paints and sunscreens.
22.fact: It is as strong as steel but weighs about 40% less.

23.uses: Steel additive (ferrovanadium) for tools and springs, and catalyst in sulfuric acid production.
23.fact: It is named after Vanadís, the Norse goddess of beauty, for the vivid colors of its compounds.

24.uses: Stainless steel, chrome plating, pigments and leather tanning.
24.fact: The red of rubies and the green of emeralds come from small amounts of chromium.

25.uses: Steel production (nearly 90% of manganese), alkaline batteries and aluminum alloys.
25.fact: Manganese dioxide was already used as a black pigment in prehistoric cave paintings.

26.uses: Steel for construction, cars, tools and machinery: it is the most widely used metal in the world.
26.fact: Hemoglobin uses iron to carry oxygen in the blood.

27.uses: Permanent magnets (alnico), turbine superalloys, lithium-ion batteries and blue pigments.
27.fact: Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy and to sterilize medical equipment.

28.uses: Stainless steel, coins, rechargeable batteries and catalyst for hydrogenating oils.
28.fact: Together with iron, it makes up most of Earth's core.

29.uses: Electrical wiring, plumbing, motors, coins and alloys such as bronze and brass.
29.fact: The Statue of Liberty's green color is a patina that formed on its copper.

30.uses: Galvanizing steel against corrosion, brass, batteries and sunscreen (zinc oxide).
30.fact: It is an essential nutrient: over 300 enzymes in the human body need it.

31.uses: Semiconductors (gallium arsenide and nitride) for LEDs, lasers and solar panels.
31.fact: It melts at about 30 °C: it liquefies in the palm of your hand.

32.uses: Fiber optics, infrared lenses for night vision and electronics; the first transistors were made of germanium.
32.fact: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-silicon' in 1871, fifteen years before it was discovered.

33.uses: Semiconductors (gallium arsenide), wood preservatives and some medicines.
33.fact: At normal pressure it does not melt: it goes straight from solid to gas (sublimes).

34.uses: Photocells, glass decolorizing, photocopiers and nutritional supplements.
34.fact: It conducts electricity better the more light it receives, a key property of early photocopiers.

35.uses: Flame retardants, water treatment, pharmaceuticals and oil-drilling fluids.
35.fact: It is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.

36.uses: High-performance lamps, high-speed photographic flashes and lasers.
36.fact: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined using a spectral line of krypton-86.

37.uses: Atomic clocks, photocells, special glasses and quantum physics research.
37.fact: In 1995 the first Bose–Einstein condensate, a new state of matter, was created with rubidium.

38.uses: Red fireworks and flares, ferrite magnets and toothpaste for sensitive teeth.
38.fact: It is named after Strontian, a Scottish village where the mineral containing it was found.

39.uses: Red phosphors in displays and LEDs, YAG lasers and high-temperature superconductors.
39.fact: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.

40.uses: Fuel cladding in nuclear reactors, ceramics, dental prostheses and cubic zirconia jewelry.
40.fact: It absorbs very few neutrons, so the nuclear industry uses nearly 90% of the zirconium produced.

41.uses: Niobium–titanium superconducting magnets (MRI, particle accelerators), special steels and jewelry.
41.fact: In the United States it was called 'columbium' for over a century; IUPAC adopted the name niobium in 1949.

42.uses: High-strength steels, refinery catalysts and molybdenum disulfide lubricants.
42.fact: The bacteria that fix nitrogen in legume roots need molybdenum in their enzymes.

43.uses: Medical imaging: technetium-99m is used in tens of millions of scans every year.
43.fact: It was the first element produced artificially; its name comes from the Greek technetos, 'artificial'.

44.uses: Wear-resistant electrical contacts, hard disk drives, catalysts and platinum alloys.
44.fact: It is named after Ruthenia, the Latin name for Russia, where it was isolated from Ural platinum ore.

45.uses: Car catalytic converters that reduce nitrogen oxides, mirrors, reflectors and jewelry plating.
45.fact: It is one of the rarest and most expensive metals in the world.

46.uses: Car catalytic converters, electronics, dentistry and jewelry (white gold).
46.fact: At room temperature it can absorb up to about 900 times its own volume of hydrogen.

47.uses: Jewelry and silverware, electrical contacts, mirrors, solar panels and antibacterial dressings.
47.fact: It is the best conductor of electricity and heat of all metals.

48.uses: Nickel–cadmium batteries (now being phased out), yellow and red pigments, and anti-corrosion coatings.
48.fact: It is highly toxic: cadmium pollution caused itai-itai disease in 20th-century Japan.

49.uses: Touchscreens and LCDs (indium tin oxide), low-melting solders and semiconductors.
49.fact: It is named after the bright indigo line in its spectrum.

50.uses: Tinplate for cans, electronic solders, bronze (with copper) and flat-glass manufacturing.
50.fact: Bending a tin bar produces a characteristic crackling sound known as the 'tin cry'.

51.uses: Flame retardants, lead alloys for batteries and semiconductors.
51.fact: In ancient Egypt, antimony sulfide was used as black eye makeup.

52.uses: Cadmium telluride solar panels, steel and copper alloys, and thermoelectric devices.
52.fact: It is rarer than gold in Earth's crust, and handling it can leave a garlic smell on the breath.

53.uses: Antiseptics, iodized salt, X-ray contrast agents and thyroid medicine.
53.fact: Its dark crystals give off a violet vapor when heated; its name means 'violet' in Greek.

54.uses: Car headlights, camera flashes, satellite ion thrusters and general anesthesia.
54.fact: In 1962 it became the first noble gas to form a chemical compound.

55.uses: Atomic clocks, oil-drilling fluids and photoelectric cells.
55.fact: The SI second is defined by a transition of the cesium-133 atom.

56.uses: Contrast agent for digestive-tract X-rays, green fireworks and drilling fluids.
56.fact: Barium sulfate is so insoluble that it can be swallowed safely to image the stomach with X-rays.

57.uses: Camera lenses, nickel–metal hydride batteries in hybrid cars and refinery catalysts.
57.fact: It gives its name to the lanthanide series; from the Greek lanthanein, 'to lie hidden'.

58.uses: Car catalytic converters, glass polishing and lighter flints (ferrocerium).
58.fact: It is the most abundant lanthanide in Earth's crust.

59.uses: Powerful magnets together with neodymium, protective goggles for welders and yellow glass.
59.fact: Its name means 'green twin': it was separated from its 'twin', neodymium, in 1885.

60.uses: Neodymium magnets for electric motors, headphones, hard drives and wind turbines; lasers.
60.fact: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets manufactured.

61.uses: Luminous paints, long-life nuclear batteries and thickness-gauging instruments.
61.fact: All its isotopes are radioactive: only minute traces exist in Earth's crust.

62.uses: Heat-resistant samarium–cobalt magnets and treatment of bone pain in cancer patients.
62.fact: It is named after the mineral samarskite, itself named after Russian engineer Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.

63.uses: Red and blue phosphors in displays and lamps, and security marks that glow under ultraviolet light.
63.fact: Euro banknotes contain luminescent europium compounds as an anti-counterfeiting measure.

64.uses: MRI contrast agents, nuclear control rods and memory devices.
64.fact: It is magnetic like iron only below about 20 °C: a hot day takes its magnetism away.

65.uses: Green phosphors in displays, electric motor magnets and materials that change shape in a magnetic field.
65.fact: It is another of the four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.

66.uses: High-temperature neodymium magnets for electric cars and wind turbines, lasers and lamps.
66.fact: Its name means 'hard to get' in Greek, because isolating it was so laborious.

67.uses: Medical holmium lasers, pole pieces for very strong magnets and spectrophotometer calibration.
67.fact: It is named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.

68.uses: Fiber-optic amplifiers, dermatological lasers and pink-tinted glass.
68.fact: Erbium-doped amplifiers let the internet cross oceans through fiber-optic cables.

69.uses: Portable X-ray devices and surgical lasers.
69.fact: It is one of the scarcest lanthanides; its name comes from Thule, the mythical far north.

70.uses: Optical atomic clocks, industrial lasers and stainless steel additive.
70.fact: Ytterbium optical clocks are among the most precise instruments ever built.

71.uses: PET scanner detectors, refinery catalysts and tumor therapy with lutetium-177.
71.fact: It is named after Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris.

72.uses: Nuclear control rods, turbine superalloys and insulators in modern chips.
72.fact: It is named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, where it was discovered.

73.uses: Capacitors in phones and computers, surgical implants and chemical-industry equipment.
73.fact: It is named after Tantalus of Greek mythology, because it barely reacts with acids.

74.uses: Incandescent lamp filaments, tungsten carbide cutting tools and counterweights.
74.fact: It has the highest melting point of all metals: about 3400 °C.

75.uses: Superalloys for jet engine turbines and catalysts for producing high-octane gasoline.
75.fact: It was the last naturally occurring non-radioactive element to be discovered, in 1925.

76.uses: Fountain pen tips, electrical contacts and very hard alloys.
76.fact: It is the densest element: a liter of osmium would weigh over 22 kilograms.

77.uses: Long-life spark plugs, high-temperature crucibles and platinum alloys.
77.fact: An iridium-rich layer from 66 million years ago supports the asteroid hypothesis for the dinosaurs' extinction.

78.uses: Car catalytic converters, jewelry, sensors and anticancer drugs such as cisplatin.
78.fact: Until 2019, the kilogram was defined by a platinum–iridium cylinder kept near Paris.

79.uses: Jewelry, monetary reserves, electronic contacts and dentistry.
79.fact: It is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet of more than half a square meter.

80.uses: Fluorescent lamps, switches and scientific instruments; its use is restricted because of its toxicity.
80.fact: It is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

81.uses: Infrared detectors, cardiac perfusion imaging (thallium-201) and special optical glass.
81.fact: Its name comes from the Greek thallos, 'green shoot', for the bright green line in its spectrum.

82.uses: Car batteries, shielding against X-rays and radiation, and counterweights; dropped from gasoline and paint because of its toxicity.
82.fact: The symbol Pb comes from the Latin plumbum, which is also the root of the word 'plumber'.

83.uses: Stomach medicines, cosmetics and a non-toxic replacement for lead in alloys and shot.
83.fact: It is slightly radioactive, but its half-life is over a billion times the age of the universe.

84.uses: Static eliminators in industry and, in the past, heat sources in satellites.
84.fact: Marie Curie named it after Poland, her native country.

85.uses: Research into cancer therapies using astatine-211.
85.fact: No visible sample has ever been seen: it would vaporize from the heat of its own radioactivity.

86.uses: Geological research and, in the past, radiotherapy; today it is measured in homes for health reasons.
86.fact: When it builds up in basements and homes, it is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

87.uses: Scientific research only: it is so unstable that no visible amount has ever been collected.
87.fact: Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939: it was the last element found in nature.

88.uses: Prostate cancer treatment with radium-223; it was once used in luminous paints.
88.fact: In the 20th century watch dials were painted with radium, and many workers who handled it became seriously ill.

89.uses: Neutron sources and targeted cancer therapy with actinium-225.
89.fact: It glows with a bluish light in the dark because of its intense radioactivity.

90.uses: Welding electrodes, magnesium alloys and a potential nuclear reactor fuel.
90.fact: It is named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder.

91.fact: It is one of the scarcest and hardest-to-isolate naturally occurring elements.

92.uses: Fuel for nuclear power plants; depleted uranium is used in armor and counterweights.
92.fact: The half-life of uranium-238 is about 4.5 billion years, close to the age of the Earth.

93.uses: Neutron detectors and production of plutonium-238.
93.fact: It was named after the planet Neptune, the next one after Uranus.

94.uses: Nuclear fuel and plutonium-238 generators for space probes.
94.fact: The Voyager probes are still sending data thanks to the heat of their plutonium-238.

95.uses: Ionization smoke detectors (americium-241) and radiation sources for industrial gauges.
95.fact: There is probably americium in your home: it is inside many smoke detectors.

96.uses: Alpha-particle sources for spectrometers, such as those on Mars rovers.
96.fact: It is named in honor of Marie and Pierre Curie.

97.uses: Research and production of heavier elements such as tennessine.
97.fact: It is named after Berkeley, the Californian city where it was synthesized.

98.uses: Neutron sources for starting reactors, prospecting for gold and oil, and treating some tumors.
98.fact: A single microgram of californium-252 emits millions of neutrons per second.

99.uses: Se descubrió en 1952 en los restos de la primera bomba de hidrógeno; su nombre honra a Albert Einstein.
99.fact: It was discovered in 1952 in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb; it is named after Albert Einstein.

100.uses: También apareció en los restos de la primera bomba de hidrógeno; su nombre honra a Enrico Fermi.
100.fact: It also turned up in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb; it is named after Enrico Fermi.

101.uses: Fue el primer elemento sintetizado de a un átomo por vez; su nombre honra a Dmitri Mendeléyev.
101.fact: It was the first element synthesized one atom at a time; it is named after Dmitri Mendeleev.

102.uses: Su nombre honra a Alfred Nobel; su descubrimiento se disputó durante años entre Suecia, Estados Unidos y la URSS.
102.fact: It is named after Alfred Nobel; its discovery was disputed for years between Sweden, the United States and the USSR.

103.uses: Su nombre honra a Ernest Lawrence, inventor del ciclotrón.
103.fact: It is named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.

104.uses: Su nombre honra a Ernest Rutherford y fue objeto de disputa durante la Guerra Fría.
104.fact: It is named after Ernest Rutherford, and its name was disputed during the Cold War.

105.uses: Su nombre viene de Dubna, la ciudad rusa sede del Instituto Unificado de Investigaciones Nucleares.
105.fact: It is named after Dubna, the Russian city that hosts the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research.

106.uses: Glenn Seaborg fue la primera persona en tener un elemento con su nombre estando en vida.
106.fact: Glenn Seaborg was the first person to have an element named after him while still alive.

107.uses: Su nombre honra a Niels Bohr, pionero del modelo atómico.
107.fact: It is named after Niels Bohr, a pioneer of the atomic model.

108.uses: Su nombre viene de Hassia, nombre latino del estado alemán de Hesse.
108.fact: It is named after Hassia, the Latin name for the German state of Hesse.

109.uses: Su nombre honra a Lise Meitner, codescubridora de la fisión nuclear.
109.fact: It is named after Lise Meitner, co-discoverer of nuclear fission.

110.uses: Su nombre viene de Darmstadt, la ciudad alemana donde fue sintetizado.
110.fact: It is named after Darmstadt, the German city where it was synthesized.

111.uses: Su nombre honra a Wilhelm Röntgen, descubridor de los rayos X.
111.fact: It is named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays.

112.uses: Su nombre honra a Nicolás Copérnico, que propuso que la Tierra gira alrededor del Sol.
112.fact: It is named after Nicolaus Copernicus, who proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun.

113.uses: Fue el primer elemento descubierto en Asia; su nombre viene de Nihon, «Japón».
113.fact: It was the first element discovered in Asia; its name comes from Nihon, 'Japan'.

114.uses: Su nombre honra al físico Gueorgui Fliórov y al laboratorio de Dubna que lleva su nombre.
114.fact: It is named after physicist Georgy Flyorov and the Dubna laboratory that bears his name.

115.uses: Su nombre viene de la región de Moscú, donde se encuentra Dubna.
115.fact: It is named after the Moscow region, where Dubna is located.

116.uses: Su nombre honra al Laboratorio Nacional Lawrence Livermore de Estados Unidos.
116.fact: It is named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States.

117.uses: Su nombre viene de Tennessee; se sintetizó usando berkelio producido en Oak Ridge.
117.fact: It is named after Tennessee; it was synthesized using berkelium produced at Oak Ridge.

118.uses: Es el elemento más pesado conocido; su nombre honra al físico Yuri Oganessian, aún vivo cuando se lo bautizó.
118.fact: It is the heaviest known element; it is named after physicist Yuri Oganessian, who was alive when it was named.
